chapter_theme: The rule of begging: Siva himself begged with Brahma's skull and made begging the devotee's way to his feet; begging from desire is faulted, while the true ascetic is free of hunger, craving and anger and the world comes to him.
structure_note: A riddle verse faults begging from desire (1886); three verses on Siva the beggar (1887 to 1889); then the devotee's freedom from hunger and anger (1890) and the two ways of the ascetic, going to doors or staying put (1891).

1886.reading: There is a seed pot and there is one fenced field, and the ploughing was finished before noon; those who cannot lose their fear, reap that crop and eat, go begging alms for their desires.
1886.nuance: The seed pot and the fenced field are symbolic; tradition takes them as bindu and the body, or as the grace and the soul, with the work already done for the devotee. The plain point is that those who do not use what they have beg out of desire.

1887.reading: He took alms in Brahma's skull; he took alms to do unfailing dharma; he took alms showing Brahma's head; he took alms so that Brahma might become supreme.
1887.nuance: The verse draws on the story of Siva as the divine beggar who cut off Brahma's fifth head and begged with its skull. பிரமன் பரமாகவே may mean to raise Brahma, to show Brahma's pride humbled, or to show himself as the supreme beyond Brahma; it is unclear.

1888.reading: People call the Lord who spread out and created the seven worlds a beggar; why does he beg? For the devotees who think of him without end, he begged so that by begging and eating they might reach his feet.
1888.nuance: The verse makes Siva's begging a model: by begging himself he made begging a path for his devotees. இரந்துண்டு may describe the Lord or the devotees; both readings lead to the same point.

1889.reading: The Lord who stands on the way waits ready to come, waits ready to give himself as joy to the good, waits to contend as their only refuge; yet if he waits to come, they say he does not know.
1889.nuance: The verse repeats இருந்தான் (he stayed, he waited). Its last line is obscure; it may mean that people think the Lord is unaware while he only waits for them to turn to him.

1890.reading: Fiery hunger, craving and anger do not stay in the bodies of Siva's devotees; those who reach Siva do not stay even in the abundant worlds or the worlds of merit.
1890.nuance: The verse pairs two kinds of not staying: the passions do not stay in the devotee, and the devotee does not stay in any heaven earned by merit. Hunger stands with the passions here, which suits a chapter on living by alms.

1891.reading: Even those very clear in true inner knowledge go with outstretched hand to the doorstep; the ascetics who stayed without going for alms found the whole world coming to them.
1891.nuance: ஐயம் is alms, but also doubt, so ஐயம் புகாமல் may mean 'without entering for alms' or 'without doubt entering'. On the first reading the verse allows two ways for the ascetic and gives the higher place to staying put.

links.note: Both put the world's creator beside begging. The Kural says that if the maker of the world decreed that people live by begging he should wander and perish; Tirumular says the maker of the seven worlds begged himself so that his devotees could reach him by begging. The conflict holds if the Kural is read as condemning all living by alms, not only the beggary of the poor.

Both fault begging that comes from desire when the remedy lies within: the Naladiyar asks why one should beg of strangers when poverty can be ended by asking of oneself, Tirumular faults those who beg for their desires instead of reaping the field already ploughed.
The Kural says pain ends when desire, anger and confusion are gone; Tirumular says hunger, craving and anger do not stay in Siva's devotees, and adds that they pass beyond the heavens too.
Both use வர இருந்தான் (waiting so as to come or be come to): in 1889 the Lord waits on the way, in 1891 the ascetic waits and the world comes to him.
